Old East Slavic

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From Proto-Slavic *pȅťь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *péktis, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷtis, from *pekʷ-. Cognates include Old Church Slavonic пещь (peštĭ) and Old Polish piec.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ˈpɛt͡ɕɪ/→/ˈpʲɛt͡ɕɪ/→/ˈpʲɛːt͡ɕ/
  • (ca. 9th CE) IPA(key): /ˈpɛt͡ɕɪ/
  • (ca. 11th CE) IPA(key): /ˈpʲɛt͡ɕɪ/
  • (ca. 13th CE) IPA(key): /ˈpʲɛːt͡ɕ/

  • Hyphenation: пе‧чь

Noun

[edit]

печь (pečĭ) f

  1. stove
  2. oven
  3. furnace

Etymology 1

[edit]

From Old East Slavic печи (peči), from Proto-Slavic *peťi, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *péktei, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷeti, from *pekʷ-.

See also English cook, culinary, cuisine, concoct and peptic; also Russian пот (pot, “sweat, perspiration”), Sanskrit पचति (pácati), Albanian pjek, Tocharian B päk-, Ancient Greek πέσσω (péssō), Latin coquō.

Verb

[edit]

печь • (pečʹ) impf (perfective испе́чь or спечь)

  1. to bake
    • 1859, Иван Гончаров [Ivan Goncharov], “Часть 3. Глава 12”, in Обломов; English translation from Marian Schwartz, transl., Oblomov, New York: Seven Stories Press, 2008:
      — Сего́дня воскре́сенье, — говори́л ла́сково го́лос, — пиро́г пекли́; не уго́дно ли закуси́ть?
      — Sevódnja voskrésenʹje, — govoríl láskovo gólos, — piróg peklí; ne ugódno li zakusítʹ?
      “Today’s Sunday,” a kindly voice said. “We baked a pie. Don’t you want to try it?”
  2. to scorch (only in relation to the Sun or other stars)

Etymology 2

[edit]

From Old East Slavic печь (pečĭ), from Proto-Slavic *peťь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *péktis, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷtis, from *pekʷ-. Doublet of пещь (peščʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

English Wikipedia has an article on:
Russian oven
Wikipedia

Noun

[edit]

печь • (pečʹ) f inan (genitive пе́чи, nominative plural пе́чи, genitive plural пече́й, relational adjective печно́й, diminutive печу́рка)

  1. stove
    Synonym: пе́чка (péčka)
  2. oven
  3. furnace
    кали́льная печь ― kalílʹnaja pečʹ ― heating/calcining furnace; calciner
  4. kiln
